  "title": "Cross-Trajectory Segment Stitching for Tool-Use Agent SFT",
  "core_problem": "Agent SFT requires high-quality demonstration trajectories, but even frontier models fail frequently on tool-use benchmarks (ToolBench pass@1 ~55% for GPT-4o, WebArena SOTA ~71.6%). Current data curation faces a fundamental quality ceiling: best-of-N selection is bounded by the quality of individual trajectories and cannot synthesize a demonstration better than the best one observed, even when stronger sub-sequences exist across rollouts. Recent work has explored step-level and segment-level approaches to improve training data quality—WebSTAR (arXiv:2512.10962) filters out bad steps, STeCa regenerates weak steps via LLM, SALT (EACL 2026) builds trajectory graphs for step-level RL advantages, TSR (arXiv:2602.11767) constructs superior rollouts via per-turn best-of-N for RL, HISR (arXiv:2603.18683) assigns segment-level process rewards for RL—but no existing method performs offline cross-trajectory segment composition for SFT: replacing weak segments with empirically validated strong alternatives from other rollouts of the same task. Critically, this gap persists despite multiple independent validations of the segment-over-rollouts abstraction in RL (SALT, TSR, HISR), suggesting the abstraction is sound but has not been applied to offline SFT data construction. The composition-over-selection paradigm is the core contribution: it creates training trajectories that exceed any individual rollout's quality ceiling while preserving trajectory completeness and grounding replacements in real execution traces. Validating this claim requires isolating composition quality from data quantity: stitched trajectories must replace originals at constant training set size, not merely augment them, to demonstrate that composition produces qualitatively better training data rather than benefiting from increased data volume. Moreover, composition and selection are complementary—TSS operates on top of best-of-N selection, potentially stacking gains—and produces qualitatively different training signals (novel sub-goal transition patterns) that no amount of selection can produce regardless of N. As a secondary hypothesis, we measure whether TSS's segment-level recombination incidentally affects interface robustness (arXiv:2602.01611 shows trajectory-SFT amplifies interface shortcutting), though we do not claim a strong mechanism for this—PIPE-style evaluation tests whether any effect exists, without assuming one.",
  "opportunity": "Multiple 2025–2026 works recognize the value of improving trajectory-level training data, and a convergent thread validates the segment-over-rollouts abstraction—but exclusively for RL, leaving offline SFT composition as an open gap. WebSTAR (arXiv:2512.10962, Dec 2025) performs step-level filtering for computer use agents: a process reward model (StepRM, 7B) grades individual actions, retaining only correct steps. Trained on 13.3K trajectories (267K graded steps), a 7B model surpasses UI-TARS-1.5-7B by >15% on WebVoyager. Key difference from TSS: WebSTAR removes suboptimal steps (losing trajectory completeness), while TSS replaces weak segments with execution-grounded alternatives (preserving completeness). STeCa (ACL 2025 Findings) calibrates weak steps by LLM regeneration, but introduces hallucination risk since regenerated steps lack execution grounding. AgentHER (arXiv:2603.21357) relabels failed trajectories to alternative goals (+7.1–11.7pp), expanding data quantity rather than improving per-trajectory quality. TopoCurate (arXiv:2603.01714) builds cross-trajectory topology but only selects existing trajectories. SALT (arXiv:2510.20022, EACL 2026 Findings) constructs trajectory graphs from multi-rollout data for step-level RL advantage estimation, validating the graph-over-rollouts paradigm but targeting RL, not offline SFT composition. TSR (arXiv:2602.11767, ICLR 2026 Workshop) constructs superior trajectories via per-turn best-of-N selection during RL training (+15% on WebShop via beam search), demonstrating that per-sub-part selection across rollouts substantially improves training trajectories—but operates at turn-level granularity for online RL, not segment-level for offline SFT. HISR (arXiv:2603.18683) decomposes trajectories into sub-goal-aligned segments and assigns segment-level process rewards using a hindsight modulation mechanism, tested on ALFWorld/VirtualHome/WebShop—independently validating sub-goal-aligned segmentation as a productive abstraction for trajectory quality, but for RL reward modeling rather than SFT data construction. CLEANER (arXiv:2601.15141) performs intra-trajectory self-purification by replacing failed segments with the model's own self-corrections—but only within a single trajectory, not across rollouts, limiting replacement quality to what the same rollout produced. TrajFusion (arXiv:2602.04391) composes across trajectories but for math reasoning with interleaved error-correction format, not sub-goal-aligned segment replacement for tool-use agents. The gap TSS fills: no existing method performs offline cross-trajectory segment composition for tool-use agent SFT—replacing weak segments with execution-grounded strong alternatives from other rollouts, preserving trajectory completeness while exceeding any individual trajectory's quality ceiling. The convergent validation of segment-over-rollouts in RL by SALT, TSR, and HISR strengthens this opportunity: the abstraction is proven productive, and TSS is the first to apply it to offline SFT data construction. This positions TSS in a clear design space: WebSTAR _removes_ bad steps (loses information), STeCa _regenerates_ bad steps (introduces hallucination risk), TSR _selects_ best turns online for RL (not offline SFT), HISR _scores_ segments for RL rewards (not SFT composition), TSS _replaces_ bad segments with empirically validated alternatives from other rollouts for offline SFT (preserves completeness with grounded replacements).",
  "landscape": "**Step-level trajectory curation for agent SFT.** WebSTAR (arXiv:2512.10962, Dec 2025) introduces step-level filtering for computer use agents: a process reward model (StepRM, 7B) grades individual actions, retaining only correct steps. Trained on 13.3K trajectories (267K graded steps), a 7B model surpasses UI-TARS-1.5-7B by >15% on WebVoyager. Key difference from TSS: WebSTAR removes suboptimal steps (losing trajectory completeness), while TSS replaces weak segments with execution-grounded alternatives (preserving completeness). STEVE (arXiv:2503.12532, March 2025) similarly performs step verification for computer-use agents using GPT-4o binary labels—complementary infrastructure that could inform TSS's segment scoring. STeCa (ACL 2025 Findings, arXiv:2502.14276) calibrates individual steps within single trajectories via LLM regeneration—regenerated steps lack execution grounding, risking hallucinated API responses.

**Cross-trajectory structure for agents.** TopoCurate (arXiv:2603.01714, March 2026) projects multi-trial rollouts into a unified semantic quotient topology, selecting trajectories via process-aware metrics (Reflective Recovery, Semantic Efficiency, Strategic Diversity). Critical difference: TopoCurate selects from existing trajectories—it cannot produce demonstrations exceeding any individual rollout's quality ceiling. TSS composes novel trajectories by replacing weak segments with strong alternatives from other rollouts. SALT (arXiv:2510.20022, EACL 2026 Findings) constructs trajectory graphs from same-prompt rollouts for step-level advantage assignment in group-based RL (GRPO plugin), tested on WebShop, ALFWorld, AppWorld. SALT independently validates the graph-over-rollouts paradigm that TSS uses for cross-trajectory alignment, but targets online RL advantage estimation rather than offline SFT data construction.

**Per-turn and segment-level trajectory construction for RL.** TSR (arXiv:2602.11767, ICLR 2026 Workshop) constructs superior trajectories by performing per-turn best-of-N selection across multiple rollouts using tree-style search (best-of-N, beam search, shallow lookahead), achieving +7–15% on WebShop with Qwen2.5-3B. The core insight—constructing better trajectories by selecting best sub-parts across rollouts rather than selecting whole trajectories—is shared with TSS. Key differences: TSR operates at turn-level granularity during online RL training (modifying rollout generation within the RL loop), while TSS operates at segment-level (sub-goal) granularity for offline SFT data construction. TSR requires environment interaction during construction; TSS composes from pre-collected rollouts. TSR is optimizer-agnostic within RL; TSS produces augmented SFT data usable by any fine-tuning framework. HISR (arXiv:2603.18683, March 2026) explicitly decomposes trajectories into sub-goal-aligned segments using GPT-4o and assigns segment-level process rewards via a Segmental Process Reward Model (SPRM) with hindsight modulation, tested on ALFWorld, VirtualHome, and WebShop. The sub-goal-aligned segmentation closely mirrors TSS's Stage 2, and HISR independently validates that segment-level (rather than turn-level) granularity captures meaningful task structure. Key difference: HISR uses segmentation for RL reward modeling (credit assignment), while TSS uses it for offline SFT data composition (segment replacement). The convergent adoption of segment-over-rollouts by SALT, TSR, and HISR in RL contexts strengthens TSS's premise: the abstraction is independently validated as productive, and TSS is the first to apply it to offline SFT composition.

**Trajectory-level data construction for agents.** AgentHER (arXiv:2603.21357, March 2026) relabels failed trajectories to alternative goals (+7.1–11.7pp on WebArena/ToolBench across 4 model families)—orthogonal to TSS (relabels goals vs. recomposes trajectories) and potentially combinable. Notably, AgentHER uses an equal-volume control (SFT-Random with the same 3,000 failed trajectories) to isolate relabeling quality from data volume effects, with 3 random seeds and human evaluation of 200 relabeling decisions (97.7% precision)—methodological precedents TSS follows for its own experimental controls. HSL (ICLR 2026) performs hindsight goal relabeling on ALFWorld with 4× data efficiency. ASTRA (arXiv:2601.21558, Jan 2026) synthesizes tool-use trajectories from tool-call graph topology with SFT + online RL, achieving SOTA at comparable scales. ASTRA generates new trajectories from graph structure; TSS composes from existing rollouts—complementary approaches. COVERT-RL (arXiv:2604.09813, April 2026) synthesizes tool-use trajectories for RL environments, not offline SFT composition. CLEANER (arXiv:2601.15141, Jan 2026) performs intra-trajectory self-purification via Similarity-Aware Adaptive Rollback (SAAR)—replacing failed segments with the model's own self-corrections within the same trajectory for agentic RL. TSS differs by performing cross-trajectory replacement for SFT, drawing better segments from other rollouts rather than relying on the same trajectory's self-corrections.

**Cross-trajectory composition in adjacent domains.** TrajFusion (arXiv:2602.04391, Feb 2026) fuses incorrect and correct trajectories with reflection prompts for math reasoning SFT—interleaved error-correction format rather than sub-goal-aligned segment replacement. SE-Agent (NeurIPS 2025, arXiv:2508.02085) performs cross-trajectory recombination via evolutionary search at inference time on code agents—fundamentally different from offline SFT data construction.

**Segment-level optimization.** SDPO (ACL 2025, arXiv:2501.01821) performs segment-level DPO for social agents. SPO (arXiv:2505.23564, May 2025) introduces segment-level credit assignment for RL with flexible segment partitioning and segment advantage estimation (+6–12pp on math benchmarks). Both validate the segment granularity but operate in RL/preference optimization, not SFT data construction.

**Interface shortcutting.** 'What Do Agents Learn from Trajectory-SFT' (arXiv:2602.01611, Feb 2026) demonstrates that trajectory-SFT amplifies interface shortcutting—agents memorize surface-level interface tokens (API names, argument formats, action syntax) rather than learning semantic tool use. Degradation reaches up to WebShop: 61.2%→4.4% under minimal interface rewrites. The paper's mitigations include per-tool decomposition and 'loose environments.' We include PIPE-style evaluation to measure whether TSS has any incidental effect on interface robustness, but we do not claim TSS directly addresses interface shortcutting, as the mechanism (interface token memorization) is distinct from what TSS modifies (segment composition).

**Offline RL trajectory stitching.** DiffStitch (ICML 2024), CompDiffuser (NeurIPS 2025 Spotlight, arXiv:2503.05153), SCoTS (arXiv:2506.00895), and STITCH-OPE (arXiv:2505.20781) operate on continuous state-action vectors in robotic/control domains, not on natural-language agent trajectories with discrete API calls.

**Trajectory diversity.** TDScaling (arXiv:2602.03219, Feb 2026) shows trajectory diversity scales better than quantity for code agents; TSS's single-segment replacement produces modest diversity gains compared to diverse prompting strategies—TSS's primary contribution is quality improvement (exceeding individual rollout ceilings), not diversity expansion. AOI (arXiv:2603.03378) and UI-Voyager GRSD (arXiv:2603.24533) correct individual failed steps. CSO (arXiv:2602.03412) optimizes verified critical steps.",
  "approach": "We propose Trajectory Segment Stitching (TSS), a streamlined offline data augmentation pipeline for tool-use agent SFT, targeting EMNLP 2026 (ARR May 25, 2026). The core thesis is that cross-trajectory composition produces measurably better training data than trajectory selection—demonstrating that the quality ceiling of individual rollouts is a real and addressable bottleneck for agent SFT. Unlike a mere proof-of-concept, TSS opens a research direction: if even single-segment replacement yields gains over best-of-10 selection, it motivates more sophisticated composition methods (multi-segment, iterative stitching, learned composition). The pipeline uses LangGraph for trajectory collection and has four core stages:

(1) **Trajectory Collection via LangGraph**: Build a LangGraph-based agent workflow. Collect N=10 rollouts per task using GPT-4o as teacher on two benchmarks: (a) **StableToolBench** (200-task subset covering single-tool and multi-tool, using StableToolBench's Virtual API Server for reproducibility—addressing the known 55.6% API instability in original ToolBench), and (b) **τ-bench retail domain** (50-task subset for cross-benchmark validation, using its structured tool-call + user-interaction format). LangGraph's built-in state management and LangSmith tracing provide structured trajectory logging.

(2) **Sub-goal Decomposition & Segment Scoring**: Leverage DFSDT's natural tree structure (StableToolBench) and user-turn boundaries (τ-bench) for sub-goal identification. Each trajectory is decomposed into 2–4 sub-goal-aligned segments—a granularity independently validated by HISR (arXiv:2603.18683), which demonstrates via GPT-4o segmentation that >50% of segments span multiple turns and align with meaningful task milestones. Each segment is scored by: (a) sub-goal achievement (API return codes, response validity, JSON schema validation), (b) action efficiency (redundant/retry call ratio), (c) error absence. Scoring uses combined heuristic signals and LLM-judged quality (Qwen3-14B). This segment scoring infrastructure draws on the same intuition as STEVE's step verification and WebSTAR's step-level grading, but operates at the segment (sub-goal) granularity rather than individual steps, and scores are used for cross-trajectory alignment rather than filtering.

(3) **Cross-Trajectory Alignment & Partial Stitching**: Segments are aligned across rollouts via semantic similarity of canonical sub-goal descriptions extracted by the LLM judge—analogous to SALT's trajectory graph construction and TSR's per-turn alignment, but at segment granularity for offline SFT composition rather than turn-level RL rollout generation. The primary stitching strategy identifies the weakest-scored segment in an otherwise-good trajectory and replaces it with the best-matching segment from another rollout, limiting boundary issues to exactly 2 transition points. This is strictly partial stitching—no full recomposition. Unlike CLEANER's intra-trajectory self-purification (replacing failures with self-corrections from the same trajectory), TSS draws replacement segments from the best-performing rollouts across all trials, accessing a larger pool of high-quality alternatives.

(4) **LLM-Based Boundary Validation**: An LLM validator (Qwen3-14B) checks state-transition consistency at the 2 segment boundaries: does the preceding segment's final state (API responses, extracted entities) provide the inputs expected by the replacement segment? Does the replacement segment's output state support the subsequent segment's actions? Stitched trajectories failing validation are discarded. We acknowledge the potential bias of using Qwen3-14B as both boundary validator and fine-tuning student. This is acceptable because the validator judges structured state-transition compatibility (API response consistency, entity availability)—a verifiable, narrowly-scoped task distinct from the open-ended trajectory generation the student learns during SFT. The validator does not assess trajectory quality or preference, which would create a self-reinforcing bias; it checks factual consistency of state (e.g., 'does entity X extracted in segment A appear in segment B's API calls?').

**Boundary Validator Evaluation (Pilot, Days 1–3)**: Two annotators independently evaluate 100 randomly sampled validator decisions (50 accepted stitches, 50 rejected stitches) for correctness, reporting precision, recall, and inter-annotator agreement (Cohen's κ). Target: validator precision ≥ 80% (ensuring < 20% training data corruption from false positives). If precision falls below 80%, we tighten validation criteria or substitute GPT-4o as validator. During the pilot, we additionally run GPT-4o validation on the same 100 boundary decisions, comparing precision/recall against Qwen3-14B to assess whether a stronger validator improves boundary judgment without requiring full SFT ablation. Preliminary precision/recall results will be reported in the methodology section to provide empirical grounding for the pipeline's reliability.

**Impact Argument — Beyond Proof-of-Concept**: The complexity of the 4-stage pipeline is justified by three arguments beyond marginal accuracy gains: (a) **Complementarity**: composition operates on top of selection—TSS is applied after best-of-N filtering, so gains stack rather than compete. AgentHER's +7–11pp via goal relabeling is orthogonal and combinable with TSS: AgentHER expands data quantity by relabeling failed trajectories to alternative goals, while TSS improves per-trajectory quality by composing stronger demonstrations from successful rollouts. A combined TSS+AgentHER condition is a natural extension. (b) **Qualitative novelty**: composition creates training signals that selection fundamentally cannot—novel sub-goal transition patterns where segment A from rollout i connects to segment B from rollout j. No amount of increasing N in best-of-N can produce these transitions if they never co-occur in a single rollout. (c) **Ceiling demonstration**: even +2pp over best-of-10 selection empirically proves that individual rollout quality is a binding constraint, motivating future work on more sophisticated composition (multi-segment replacement, learned stitching policies, iterative refinement). The scientific contribution is establishing composition-over-selection as a viable paradigm, not maximizing a single benchmark number.

**Replace-vs-Augment Experimental Design**: To isolate composition quality from data quantity effects, our primary comparison holds training set size constant, following the equal-volume control principle demonstrated by AgentHER (arXiv:2603.21357, which uses SFT-Random with the same 3,000 trajectories to isolate relabeling quality). Three conditions: (a) **best-of-N** (N trajectories, selected from 10 rollouts—the strongest single-trajectory selection baseline), (b) **TSS-replace** (N trajectories, where stitched versions replace their source originals—same training set size, higher per-trajectory quality), (c) **TSS-augment** (N+M trajectories, stitched trajectories added alongside originals—secondary condition measuring the additional benefit of increased data volume from composition). Only if TSS-replace > best-of-N is the quality improvement claim supported; if only TSS-augment > best-of-N, the gain could be attributed to data quantity rather than quality. This three-condition design is the minimum experimental control needed to validate the composition-over-selection thesis. We explicitly frame the contribution: 'To isolate composition quality from data quantity, our primary comparison holds training set size constant.'

**Sensitivity Analysis for Expected Improvement**: Among best-of-10 selected trajectories, we estimate ~35% contain at least one clearly suboptimal segment (unnecessary retries, roundabout API calls, partial failures that get recovered). In the TSS-replace setting, improvement comes from substituting higher-quality stitched trajectories for originals in a size-constant training set:
- If validity is 30%: ~10% of trajectories improved → expected gain +1–2pp over best-of-N
- If validity is 50%: ~17% of trajectories improved → expected gain +2–4pp
- If validity is 70%: ~24% of trajectories improved → expected gain +3–6pp
At any viable validity rate, the composition-over-selection paradigm is demonstrated. Even at the conservative 30% validity scenario, the +1–2pp gain over best-of-10 selection (which itself already uses 10× the compute of single-rollout selection) establishes that the quality ceiling is real.

**Diversity Expectations (Calibrated)**: We acknowledge that single-segment replacement produces modest diversity gains—each stitched trajectory shares ~75% of segments with its source. TSS's primary contribution is quality improvement (exceeding individual rollout ceilings), not diversity expansion. We report Jaccard similarity of action sequences and unique action n-gram counts as quantitative measures, but frame these as characterizing the nature of TSS's modifications rather than claiming large diversity gains. For diversity-focused scaling, methods like TDScaling's diverse prompting strategies are more appropriate; TSS addresses a complementary axis (extracting maximum quality from existing rollouts).

**Pilot Study (Days 1–3)**: Before committing to the full pipeline, run a feasibility study on 20 StableToolBench tasks (10 rollouts each). Inspect: (a) sub-goal sharing across rollouts (target: >60% of task pairs share ≥2 sub-goals), (b) stitching validity rate after LLM validation (target: >30% viable, >50% ideal), (c) action-sequence Jaccard distance between stitched and source trajectories (to quantify actual diversity contribution), (d) **boundary validator precision/recall via 100 human-annotated decisions** (target: precision ≥ 80%, with Cohen's κ ≥ 0.7 for inter-annotator agreement). If pilot validity falls below 30%, pivot to **segment-quality contrastive SFT**: use TSS's scored segments to construct (good-segment, weak-segment) pairs for contrastive learning within the SFT objective—differentiated from SDPO by using cross-trajectory alignment to find segment pairs addressing the same sub-goal (not just within-trajectory segment comparisons), and differentiated from SPO by targeting offline SFT rather than online RL. Preliminary stitching validity and validator precision results from the pilot will be reported in the methodology section to add empirical grounding.

**Statistical Testing and Power Analysis**: We report mean ± std over **5 random seeds** (42, 123, 456, 789, 2026) for the 3 primary conditions (TSS-replace, TSS-augment, best-of-N) and **3 random seeds** for secondary baselines and ablations, following paired multi-seed evaluation protocol recommendations (arXiv:2511.19794). Statistical significance is assessed via **paired bootstrap resampling** (n=10,000) at the task level with p<0.05 threshold. **Minimum detectable effect (MDE)**: with the full StableToolBench solvable test set (~200+ tasks) and 5 seeds, the paired bootstrap reliably detects differences ≥3pp at p<0.05. If pilot results suggest improvements below this threshold, we increase to 7 seeds or expand to additional evaluation tasks to maintain adequate statistical power. For τ-bench (50 tasks), we report both pass^1 and pass^5; due to the smaller task count, τ-bench serves as cross-benchmark directional validation rather than primary significance testing.

**Training & Evaluation**: Fine-tune Qwen3-14B (LoRA, rank 64) on each training condition. Three evaluation dimensions:
- **Standard metrics**: StableToolBench Solvable Pass Rate (SoPR) and Solvable Win Rate (SoWR); τ-bench pass^1 and pass^5 (k=1,5).
- **Interface robustness (exploratory)**: PIPE-style evaluation on StableToolBench—minimally rewrite API names and argument formats while preserving semantics, measuring performance degradation. Evaluated on the 3 primary conditions only. This is an exploratory measurement to test whether TSS has any incidental effect on interface robustness; we do not claim a strong mechanism linking segment composition to interface token memorization, as these are distinct phenomena (arXiv:2602.01611).
- **Composition characterization**: Report Jaccard similarity of action sequences between stitched and original trajectories, unique action n-gram counts, and percentage of stitched trajectories containing sub-goal transitions absent from any individual rollout.

**Baselines, comparisons, and ablations**: Primary comparison (5 seeds each): (i) best-of-N trajectory selection (10 rollouts, select best—constant training set size N), (ii) TSS-replace (stitched replace originals—constant size N, tests quality improvement), (iii) TSS-augment (stitched added alongside—size N+M, secondary). Secondary baselines (3 seeds each): (iv) success-only SFT (standard practice), (v) step-level filtering (WebSTAR-style: remove suboptimal steps from best trajectories, providing a direct comparison of the filter-vs-replace paradigm). AgentHER is discussed as an indicative reference using their published results (+7.1–11.7pp on ToolBench); we explicitly note that TSS and AgentHER are complementary—TSS improves per-trajectory quality via composition while AgentHER expands data quantity via goal relabeling—and that a combined TSS+AgentHER condition is a promising extension for future work. Three ablations (3 seeds each): (a) segment scoring function (heuristic-only vs. combined—to isolate LLM judge contribution to segment quality assessment), (b) replacement scope (single weakest segment vs. all below-threshold segments—to measure whether additional stitching points introduce more boundary errors than quality gains), (c) boundary validator (Qwen3-14B-filtered vs. unfiltered stitching—to quantify the validator's contribution to training data quality).

**Paper Writing (Days 12–14)**: Explicitly budgeted. Days 12–13: Claude-assisted drafting of related work, methodology, and introduction (parallelized with final evaluation runs). Day 14: results integration, limitations section, final polish.",

The primary stitching strategy identifies the weakest-scored segment in an otherwise-good trajectory and replaces it with the best-matching segment from another rollout, limiting boundary issues to exactly 2 transition points.
